gotchasForJS: The wrapper itself: naive JS would `console.log(v)` and emit `1.5\n`. You MUST emit `"b'" + payload + "'\n"`. Do not use JSON.stringify on the wrapper (it would add double quotes).

Integral floats need a trailing `.0`. Python: `--a 1` -> b'1.0', `--a 100` -> b'100.0', `--a 1e10` -> b'10000000000.0'. JS `String(1)` -> "1", `String(1e10)` -> "10000000000". You must append ".0" when the decimal form has no '.' and no 'e'.
Negative zero: Python prints b'-0.0'; JS `String(-0)` is "0" and `(-0).toFixed(1)` is "0.0". You must special-case Object.is(x, -0) -> "-0.0".

Exponential threshold on the large side differs: Python switches to exponent at |x| >= 1e16 (1e15 -> "1000000000000000.0", 1e16 -> "1e+16"), while JS switches at >= 1e21 (`String(1e16)` -> "10000000000000000"). Naive JS would print b'10000000000000000.0' instead of b'1e+16'.

Exponential threshold on the small side differs: Python switches when the decimal exponent < -4 (1e-4 -> "0.0001", 1e-5 -> "1e-05"), while JS switches below 1e-6 (`String(1e-5)` -> "0.00001"). Naive JS would print b'0.00001' instead of b'1e-05'.

Exponent zero-padding: Python pads the exponent to at least 2 digits and always includes the sign — "1e-05", "1.5e-08", "1e+16". JS `(1e-7).toString()` -> "1e-7" and `(1e21).toString()` -> "1e+21" (no padding to 2 digits for single-digit exponents). You must pad: sign + String(absExp).padStart(2, '0'). Three-digit exponents are NOT padded further ("1e+308", "5e-324", "-1e-320").

Exponent mantissa form: Python's repr keeps the shortest round-trip mantissa with no forced decimal point — "1e+16", not "1.0e+16". JS `toExponential()` without an argument is close but `Number(1e16).toExponential()` gives "1e+16" (ok) while `toExponential(17)` would give trailing zeros. Use the shortest-round-trip digits (which `Number.prototype.toString()` gives) and re-assemble.
Exponent letter is always lowercase 'e' (never 'E'), matching JS, but note uppercase input `1E5` is normalized away by the parser.

Precision: Python uses shortest round-trip repr (same algorithm as JS `Number.prototype.toString`), so digit strings agree — 0.1 -> "0.1", 0.30000000000000004 -> "0.30000000000000004", 9007199254740993 -> "9007199254740992.0", 1234567890123456789 -> "1.2345678901234568e+18". Do NOT use toPrecision(17) or toFixed; those produce trailing-zero noise Python never emits.
Newline: exactly one LF. Node's `console.log` adds '\n' on Linux (fine), but if you build the string manually do not use os.EOL / '\r\n' — the observed byte is 0x0A only, even on the repr path.

No escaping / no quote-switching is ever needed. Python's repr(bytes) would switch to b"..." only if the payload contained a 0x27, and would backslash-escape bytes outside printable ASCII. The float repr charset is strictly [0-9 . e + -], so a JS port can hardcode single quotes and never implement escape logic. Do not port a generic bytes-repr escaper — it is dead code here and risks introducing differences.

Non-finite handling: inf / -inf / nan / overflow (1e400) must NOT print a wrapper. They exit 1 with a Python traceback ending in `ValueError: Out of range float values are not JSON compliant: inf` (or `: nan`) plus a `[PYI-####:ERROR] Failed to execute script 'test3' due to unhandled exception!` line. JS `JSON.stringify(Infinity)` returns "null" — a naive port would wrongly print b'null'.

Parse-error path: invalid float text exits 2 with `usage: test3_executable [-h] --a A` then `test3_executable: error: argument --a: invalid float value: '<raw>'` on stderr; a bare `-`-leading value passed as a separate token exits 2 with `error: argument --a: expected one argument`. Neither prints anything on stdout.
stderr is exactly 0 bytes on success — do not emit warnings or progress output.

Input parsing accepts Python float() syntax that JS parseFloat/Number does not: underscores (`1_000` -> b'1000.0'), leading `+`, surrounding whitespace, `1.` and `.5`, and rejects hex (`0x10` -> exit 2) which `Number('0x10')` would accept as 16.

NOTATION SELECTION: use fixed-point notation iff -4 <= E <= 15; use scientific notation iff E < -4 or E >= 16. Equivalently: fixed for 1e-4 <= |x| < 1e16, scientific for |x| < 1e-4 or |x| >= 1e16 (and for x == 0, fixed). This is Python's `%.17g`-style rule with precision 17.

SCIENTIFIC form exponent: literal 'e', then ALWAYS an explicit sign ('+' or '-'), then |E| in decimal zero-padded to a MINIMUM of 2 digits (no upper padding — 3-digit exponents print 3 digits, never 4). Formula: 'e' + (E<0?'-':'+') + String(Math.abs(E)).padStart(2,'0').

So every |x| in [1e16, 1e21) is formatted differently by naive JS. Affected examples: 1e16, 1e17, 1e18, 1e20, 12345678901234567.0, 15000000000000000.0.

THRESHOLD (small): JS `String(1e-5)` gives "0.00001" and JS only switches at 1e-7; Python switches at 1e-5 (decimal exponent <= -5). So every |x| in (1e-7, 1e-4) is formatted differently by naive JS. Affected examples: 1e-5 -> "1e-05" not "0.00001"; 1e-6 -> "1e-06" not "0.000001"; 9.999e-5 -> "9.999e-05" not "0.00009999"; 0.000012345 -> "1.2345e-05".

TRAILING '.0': JS `String(1)` is "1", `String(100)` is "100", `String(1e10)` is "10000000000". Python prints "1.0", "100.0", "10000000000.0". You must append ".0" whenever the fixed-point output has no fractional digits. This includes 0 -> "0.0".

EXPONENT ZERO-PADDING: JS never zero-pads exponents. `(1e-5).toExponential()` is "1e-5" and `String(1e-7)` is "1e-7", but Python prints "1e-05" and "1e-07". Pad |exponent| to a minimum of 2 digits. Do NOT pad beyond 2: 1e+100 / 1e-100 / 1e+308 / 5e-324 keep 3 digits.
EXPONENT SIGN: always emit an explicit '+' for positive exponents ("1e+16"). JS `toExponential()` also emits '+', but if you hand-roll from `toString()` splitting you may lose it.

NEGATIVE ZERO: JS `String(-0)` is "0" and `(-0).toFixed(1)` is "-0.0" inconsistently across paths. Python prints "-0.0". Special-case `Object.is(x, -0)` FIRST, before any zero check. Also note `--a -0` (integer-looking) still yields "-0.0".
NO '.0' IN EXPONENTIAL FORM: a single-digit mantissa must print as "1e+16", "5e-324", "1e-05" — never "1.0e+16". Do not naively reuse the fixed-point ".0"-appending logic for the scientific branch.

SIGNIFICANT DIGITS: do not use `toFixed(17)` or `toPrecision(17)`. Python uses shortest round-trip, so 0.1 -> "0.1" and 2.2250738585072011e-308 -> "2.225073858507201e-308" (16 digits, not 17). JS's zero-argument `toExponential()` and `toString()` both already produce shortest round-trip digits, so extract digits from `Math.abs(x).toExponential()` and re-lay them out yourself rather than reformatting with a fixed precision.
toPrecision/toExponential WITH an argument would add trailing zeros (e.g. `(1.5).toExponential(2)` -> "1.50e+0"); always call `toExponential()` with NO argument to get the shortest digit string.

BOUNDARY IS ON THE DECIMAL EXPONENT OF THE ROUNDED SHORTEST DIGITS, not on a raw comparison against 1e16. `9999999999999999.0` rounds to the double 1e16 and therefore prints "1e+16", while `9999999999999998.0` prints "9999999999999998.0". Deriving the exponent from `toExponential()` (as the reference implementation does) gets this right automatically; comparing `x < 1e16` before rounding could not.

INFINITY/NaN ARE NOT FORMATTED AT ALL: they must throw, not print. JS `JSON.stringify(Infinity)` yields "null" and `String(Infinity)` yields "Infinity"; this program exits 1 with a ValueError traceback (`Out of range float values are not JSON compliant: inf|-inf|nan`) and empty stdout. rules.evidence: `--a -` -> rc=2 `invalid float value: '-'` (consumed as value, then float() failed).  `--a '- 1'` -> rc=2 `invalid float value: '- 1'`.  `--a '-1e5 '` (TRAILING SPACE) -> rc=0 stdout `b'-100000.0'` — accepted!  `--a '-1e5x y'` -> rc=2 `invalid float value: '-1e5x y'`.  `--a '-abc def'` -> rc=2 `invalid float value: '-abc def'`.  `--a $'-1e5\t'` (trailing TAB) -> rc=2 `expected one argument` (tab is not a space).  `--a $'-1e5\n'` -> rc=2 `expected one argument`.

rules.rule: `--a=<value>` bypasses option detection entirely: the value after `=` is taken verbatim, so any negative-looking string works with the `=` form. Similarly a leading space or tab in the value makes it non-option-looking.

Extras are reported in argv order, verbatim, including empty strings (which contribute an empty field, producing a trailing space / double space).

rules.rule: ERROR PRECEDENCE (three tiers, in this order): (1) errors raised while scanning argv left-to-right — the help action firing, `expected one argument`, `invalid float value`, `ignored explicit argument` — win over everything and are emitted at the moment they are hit; (2) the missing-required-argument check runs after the whole scan; (3) the unrecognized-arguments check runs last, in parse_args after parse_known_args returns.

gotchasForJS: THE NEGATIVE-NUMBER REGEX IS THE #1 TRAP. A naive JS port that just does `if (arg.startsWith('-')) treatAsOption()` will reject `--a -1` and `--a -1.5`; a naive port that does `if (!isNaN(parseFloat(arg))) treatAsValue()` will WRONGLY accept `--a -1e5`, `--a -inf`, `--a -1.`. You must implement exactly: `/^-\d+$|^-\d*\.\d+$/u` (Unicode-aware \d) — and only then treat the token as a value. `-1e5`, `-1E5`, `-1.`, `-inf`, `-nan`, `-1_000`, `-1e309` MUST produce `argument --a: expected one argument`.

JS `\d` in a regex matches ONLY ASCII 0-9; Python's `\d` matches all Unicode Nd digits. So `--a -٥` -> `b'-5.0'` and `--a -٣.٥` -> `b'-3.5'` in Python. To replicate you need `/^-[\p{Nd}]+$|^-[\p{Nd}]*\.[\p{Nd}]+$/u`. Note `-1²` is REJECTED (superscript 2 is category No, not Nd).

A token containing a literal ASCII space (0x20) ANYWHERE is never treated as an option, so `--a '-1e5 '` (trailing space) SUCCEEDS with -100000.0 while `--a '-1e5'` fails. A tab or newline does NOT have this effect (`--a $'-1e5\t'` fails). JS ports usually forget this space check entirely.
The bare token `-` is a value, not an option — `--a -` gives `invalid float value: '-'`, not `expected one argument`.

`Number()`/`parseFloat` are NOT equivalent to Python `float()`. Differences you must handle: `parseFloat('1.5.5')` = 1.5 but Python rejects it; `Number('0x10')` = 16 but Python rejects it; `Number('')` = 0 and `Number(' ')` = 0 but Python rejects both; `Number('1_000')` = NaN but Python accepts it as 1000; `Number('Infinity')` = Infinity but Python needs 'inf'/'infinity' case-insensitively AND ALSO accepts 'Infinity' — Python accepts inf/infinity/nan in any case, JS `Number` only accepts exactly 'Infinity'/'-Infinity' and no 'nan'/'inf' at all; `Number('١٢٣')` = NaN but Python gives 123. Python also accepts `1e-400` as 0.0 (JS agrees) and `.5`/`5.`/`+1.5` (JS `Number` agrees).
PEP-515 underscore rules: single underscores between digits only. `1_000` and `1_000.5` OK; `1__0.5`, `1_.5`, `1._5` rejected. No JS built-in does this — write a validator.

The error-message value is Python `repr()`, not a plain single-quote wrap. If the value contains `'` but no `"`, the quotes flip to double: `--a "ab'c"` -> `invalid float value: "ab'c"`. With both quote chars present it uses single quotes with `\'` escaping. Newlines/tabs/backslashes are escaped (`\n`, `\t`, `\\`). Non-ASCII is emitted literally.

Error precedence must be replicated: the missing-required error is emitted BEFORE the unrecognized-arguments error. `-a 1.5` prints `the following arguments are required: --a`, NOT `unrecognized arguments: -a 1.5`. Most hand-rolled JS parsers report the unknown flag instead.

`-h`/`--help` short-circuits during the left-to-right scan, so `-x -h` and `-h --a abc` exit 0 with help, while `--a abc -h` exits 2 with the float error. Order matters — do not do a pre-pass for `--help` unconditionally, and do not do the required-check before scanning.

The `--` separator does NOT do what you'd expect: there are no positionals, so `--` and everything after it become extras and the `--` token itself appears verbatim in the message (`unrecognized arguments: -- extra`). Also `--a -- 1.5` does NOT give `--a` the value 1.5; it errors with `expected one argument`.

Abbreviation is asymmetric: `--h`/`--he`/`--hel` all work as `--help` (argparse allow_abbrev), but there is no `-a` short flag and `--A` is not recognized (case-sensitive). A JS port must implement prefix matching for long options.
stdout on success is the Python `repr()` of a bytes object: literally `b'1.5'` including the `b`, the single quotes, and a trailing newline. Do not print bare `1.5`.
Both `--a` and `--A` non-existence: `--a1.5` (no separator, no `=`) is NOT parsed as `--a` + `1.5`; it's an unknown option. Only `--a VALUE` and `--a=VALUE` work.

Empty-string extras still occupy a field in the join: `--a 1.5 ''` yields a line ending in `arguments: ` (trailing space before \n) and two empty extras yield two spaces. A JS `.filter(Boolean)` before joining would silently drop them.

inf/nan/overflow are NOT argparse errors: they parse successfully (exit code would be 0 from the parser) and then the program dies with exit code 1, empty stdout, and a Python traceback whose final line contains a nondeterministic PID: `[PYI-<pid>:ERROR] Failed to execute script 'test3' due to unhandled exception!`. Exit 2 vs 1 distinguishes parse errors from runtime errors.

The program name is `basename(argv[0])`, so a JS port should use `path.basename(process.argv[1])` (or hardcode `test3_executable` if argv[0] fidelity is not required). Usage/help wrapping honors the `COLUMNS` env var (default 80); error message lines are never wrapped even when the usage line is.
